# Keyboard Switch Lubing

## Overview

I lubed ninety tactile switches in one sitting, and that was the sensible number to do at once rather than a heroic one. The board is a 65% layout, so the count is small enough that a single evening covers it without my hands giving up. Lubing changes the feel more than it changes the sound, and the tactile bump on these switches becomes rounder and less scratchy once there is a thin film of grease on the right surfaces. I do it because I type all day and the difference is real, not because I enjoy the tedium. The work is repetitive and it rewards a boring routine. I set up a tray, a light, and a podcast, and I do not try to rush the middle of the pile. The first ten switches take the longest, because I am still checking every one against the recipe, and by the fiftieth my hands have the rhythm and the work speeds up on its own. I stop at the point where I would start making mistakes rather than pushing through to finish, since an over-lubed switch cannot be easily undone and the whole point of the batch is that every switch in it feels the same.

## Steps

I open every switch first and separate the parts into trays: stems in one, springs in another, bottom housings in a third. A switch opener does this in a second per switch, and trying to prise one open with a small screwdriver is how people break the little clips. The stem holder is the other tool I would not do without, because it holds a stem steady while I brush it and stops me chasing it across the desk.

For the stems I use Tribosys 3203 on the legs, which is the part that meets the tactile leaf. A light coat on the legs is what smooths the bump. I brush a thin layer over the rails as well, and I am careful never to get grease on the little silicone pads at the top of the stem, because that would kill the return. The rule I follow is that a coat should be visible but barely, a sheen rather than a smear.

For the springs I use a bag routine with 105 oil. I drop the springs into a small bag, add two or three drops of the oil, close the bag, and shake it for a minute so every spring picks up the same thin film. Then I tip them out onto a cloth and leave them for a few minutes before fitting. The bag routine is much faster than oiling springs one at a time and the result is more even. It also keeps the oil off my fingers, which matters when the next step needs dry hands.

Once the parts are ready I fit 0.15 mm films between the top and bottom housings of each switch. The film takes out the tiny wobble between the two halves and gives the switch a slightly deeper, more solid note. I do this as I close each switch, so the film cannot be forgotten. Then I press the switch closed and check that the stem moves freely and the bump is still where it should be.

I work through the whole tray in one pass, and the pass takes about three hours with a podcast on. Ninety switches at roughly two minutes each is the arithmetic, and that lines up with the time I actually spend once the setup is out of the way. I keep the finished switches in a bowl and I count them as they go in, so I know I am not missing one when the tray runs low. When the pile is done I fit them into the board, test each one in a typing tool, and set aside any that feel wrong.

## Notes

The first time I lubed switches I overdid it, and the board felt mushy for a month. The lesson was that less is more, and that the legs are the one place a slightly heavier touch is fine. The bag routine for springs came from the same lesson, since a spring with too much oil pings differently and gathers dust. I now keep a written recipe on the shelf beside the tray, so I do not have to remember ratios while my hands are greasy. I also do the work on a cloth laid over a tray, because a dropped spring is otherwise gone for good. The switches I set aside during testing usually just need their film seated better, and eight out of ten come back fine after a reseat. The mistake I made most often early on was putting films in on the wrong side, which is easy to do when the tray is full and the parts look alike; now I fit the film before the stem goes anywhere near the housing, so there is only one sensible order and I cannot get it wrong at speed. The other thing I would tell anyone starting is to count the films before starting. If the number of films and the number of switches do not match at the outset, the mismatch will find you at switch eighty-nine.

## Maintenance

There is not much to maintain. Every few months I pull the keycaps and brush the plate, since dust works its way into the gaps. If a switch starts to feel scratchy I open the board up, pull that one switch, and refresh the grease on its legs. I keep the tray and the tools in a small box so the next batch is a matter of taking the box out rather than gathering everything again. The film stock lives in that box too, so I never start a batch short of films. The grease itself keeps for years if the lid is on, and I write the date I opened each jar on the lid so I am not relying on memory. If a whole row of switches starts to feel dry at once, that is usually the grease telling me it has gone stiff, and I open a fresh jar rather than thinning the old one.
